blocks.prompt: The Cat That Runs Faster Than a Car
blocks.text: The cheetah is the fastest runner on land. No animal on Earth can beat it in a short race. Its legs are long and thin. Its back bends like a spring. Its tail swings out to help it turn. A cheetah cannot run fast for long. It runs hard for about twenty seconds. Then it gets too hot and has to stop and rest. A cheetah cannot roar like a lion. It chirps. It purrs. It sounds a lot like a very big house cat.

to help it turn
it chirps and it purrs

blocks.prompt: The Cat Built Like a Race Car
blocks.text: A cheetah is built for one job. Every part of it helps it run. Start at the feet. Most cats pull their claws all the way in. A cheetah cannot. Its claws stay out a little, all the time, and they grip the ground like the spikes on a runner's shoe. Now look at the back. A cheetah's spine bends and snaps straight again with every stride, like a bow. That flick throws the cheetah forward. At full speed, all four feet leave the ground twice in one stride. For most of a chase, the cheetah is flying. The tail does the steering. It is long and heavy and flat. The cheetah swings it out to one side to lean into a turn, the way you swing your arms on a bike. There is a price. All that work makes heat, and heat builds fast. A cheetah can only run flat out for about half a minute. Then it has to lie down and breathe. Its chase is over, win or lose.

blocks.prompt: Fast, and Paying For It
blocks.text: Everyone knows the cheetah is fast. Fewer people know what it gave up to get there. A lion is heavy, with thick bones, a wide jaw, and long teeth rooted deep in its skull. A cheetah is the opposite. It is light and slender, and its teeth are small. Those small teeth are not an accident. Big teeth need big roots, and big roots take up space in the skull. The cheetah traded that space for wide nasal passages, so it can pull in enough air to feed a sprint. Speed cost it the weapons other big cats carry. The sprint itself is brutal. A cheetah accelerates from standing to highway speed in about three seconds. Its breathing jumps from around sixty breaths a minute to more than a hundred and fifty. Its body temperature climbs. After twenty or thirty seconds it has to stop, whether or not it caught anything, and then it lies in the grass for half an hour just to cool down and recover. That half hour is dangerous. A resting cheetah cannot defend a meal. Lions and hyenas follow the dust of a chase, walk up, and take the kill. The cheetah, still panting, backs away. It cannot fight them and it cannot afford to be hurt. A limping cheetah is a starving cheetah. So the fastest animal on land spends much of its life losing its dinner to slower animals. Speed wins the chase. It does not win the argument afterward.

answers: big teeth need big roots, and the cheetah used that skull space for wide nasal passages instead, so it could breathe enough to sprint

blocks.prompt: The Big Cat That Purrs
blocks.text: Sort the world's cats into two piles and the cheetah lands in a surprising one. Lions, tigers, leopards, and jaguars can roar. They cannot purr steadily. House cats can purr steadily. They cannot roar. The difference sits in the throat, in a small structure called the hyoid and in the vocal folds attached to it. Roaring cats have a long, stretchy ligament there that can be pulled into a low, carrying boom. Purring cats have a stiffer setup that vibrates evenly on the breath in and the breath out. The cheetah purrs. It also chirps, a high, birdlike call a mother uses to gather her cubs, and it yips and growls and hisses. What it cannot do is roar. The fastest hunter in Africa announces itself with a noise closer to a sparrow than a lion. That is not the only way the cheetah stands apart. Look at its feet. Almost every cat sheathes its claws to keep them sharp for gripping prey. The cheetah's claws stay half out and stay blunt, worn down by the ground, because it needs traction more than it needs knives. Look at its face. Two black lines run from the inner eye down to the mouth. Researchers think these malar stripes cut glare from the African sun, the way an athlete smears black paint under their eyes before a game, and help the cheetah hold a fix on prey during a chase. And then there is the problem hiding in its blood. About ten thousand years ago, cheetahs came within a hair of vanishing. The survivors were so few that every cheetah alive today is descended from that tiny group. They are close to identical. You can graft a patch of skin from one wild cheetah onto another, unrelated one, and the body accepts it, because it cannot tell the difference between self and stranger. That sounds like a curiosity. It is a warning. A population with almost no genetic variation has almost no room to adapt. One new disease could move through all of them at once. Fewer than seven thousand cheetahs remain in the wild.

meta.templateLabel: The Cat That Runs Faster Than a Car

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Acinonyx jubatus
Fastest wild run recorded: about 58 mph
Brakes harder than it accelerates
Its name means the spotted one
Asiatic cheetahs survive only in Iran
Fewer than 7,000 left in the wild

blocks.prompt: Speed Is the Least Interesting Thing About a Cheetah
blocks.text: Ask anyone to name the fastest animal on land and you will get the right answer immediately. Ask where the number comes from and the room goes quiet. For most of the twentieth century, the cheetah's famous top speed rested on remarkably thin evidence. The figure of roughly seventy miles an hour traces back to a handful of runs by captive, trained cheetahs chasing a lure down a straight track, timed with the tools of the day. In 2012, a cheetah named Sarah at the Cincinnati Zoo ran one hundred meters in 5.95 seconds, faster than any human has ever covered that distance, and touched around sixty-one miles an hour on the way. Impressive, and still not an answer. A tame cat sprinting in a straight line after a rag is not a cheetah hunting. Nobody had measured the real thing. Then a team led by Alan Wilson put custom collars on five wild cheetahs in Botswana. Each collar carried GPS, accelerometers, and gyroscopes, and it recorded every stride the animal took, out in the bush, at night and in daylight, for over a year. The collars captured 367 hunting runs. What came back rearranged the story. The top speed was real but rare. The fastest single run clocked about fifty-eight miles an hour, and almost no hunt reached it. The typical chase ran at little more than half the cheetah's maximum, over a distance shorter than two football fields. If speed alone decided these hunts, the cheetah was leaving most of its talent unused. The reason sat in the other columns of data. The cheetahs were accelerating harder than any other land animal ever recorded, gaining around six miles an hour in a single stride. More striking still, they braked harder than they accelerated. A cheetah at full tilt could shed four meters per second of speed in one footfall. That is what the claws are for. A cheetah's claws never fully retract, and they are blunt, and for a hundred years that was written up as a quirk. The collars showed what it actually buys: grip, in the exact moment the animal needs to plant a foot and change everything about where it is going. And that is the hunt. An impala cannot outrun a cheetah, but it does not have to. It only has to turn faster than the cheetah can follow. So the chase is not a race. It is an argument about geometry, and the cheetah wins it by being able to slow down, hook a turn, and rebuild its speed before the impala can straighten out. Only about a quarter of the runs ended in a kill. None of this was visible from the racetrack, and that is the part worth sitting with. Scientists had studied cheetahs for generations and had measured the one thing that was easy to measure. The story that came out of that, the story every kid learns, was not wrong. It was just the least interesting true thing about the animal. It took instruments small enough to ride on a wild cat's neck to find out that the cheetah's real gift is not going fast. It is stopping.
